title: Hubble finds dark matter ring in galaxy cluster
caption: The galaxy cluster Cl 0024+17, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: ZwCl0024+1652 · constellation Pisces · about z=0.39 (redshift) away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, M.J. Jee and H. Ford (Johns Hopkins University)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Yellow galaxies crowd the foreground of this picture of the galaxy cluster Cl 0024+17, also cataloged as ZwCl 0024+1652. Around them are faint, distant background galaxies whose light has been bent by the cluster's strong gravity. One of these, about twice as far away as the yellow cluster galaxies, has been split into five separate blue arcs.

By mapping how the background light is distorted, astronomers worked out how dark matter is spread through the cluster. That is how an international team using Hubble found a ghostly ring of dark matter, thought to have formed long ago in a huge collision between two massive galaxy clusters.

It was the first time a distribution of dark matter had been found that differs substantially from that of ordinary matter. Dark matter cannot be seen directly, so its presence here is known only from the way its gravity bends light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light through six filters from 435 nm to 850 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The dark matter ring itself is invisible in any light, and the lensed background galaxies are far too faint to see without Hubble.
